notes: Seven-judge Court of Appeal on Article 8 and gypsy trespass; bound by Qazi despite Connors incompatibility.

enrichment.short_title: Maloney v Leeds: Article 8 defence to local authority possession after Connors
key_facts: The Maloney family, gypsies, occupied Leeds City Council recreational land at Spinkwell Lane without consent from June 2004.
The Council's freehold title was undisputed and the only defence pleaded was infringement of Article 8 ECHR.
The Strasbourg Court in Connors v United Kingdom had held that summary eviction from a local authority gypsy site lacked requisite procedural safeguards.
Judge Bush held he was bound by Harrow LBC v Qazi and granted leave to appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a preliminary issue in transferred possession proceedings on whether Article 8 could be raised as a defence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the court followed Qazi but indicated permission to appeal to the House of Lords might be granted to take Connors into account.
enrichment.ratio: Where a House of Lords decision on Convention rights conflicts with a subsequent Strasbourg decision, an inferior court must follow the House of Lords; Connors is incompatible with Qazi but does not permit departure from it at Court of Appeal level.
legal_issues: Whether Connors is incompatible with the majority reasoning in Qazi on Article 8 and absolute proprietary rights to possession
Whether Article 8 can be raised as a defence in county court possession proceedings against a public authority
Whether Connors is confined to gypsy site cases or has broader procedural significance
Which decision an inferior court should follow when Strasbourg and House of Lords authority conflict
linked_authorities: Harrow London Borough Council v Qazi [2003] UKHL 43
Connors v United Kingdom (2004) Application no. 66746/01
Kay v London Borough of Lambeth [2004] EWCA Civ 926

confidence.notes: Preliminary issue, Strasbourg comparison and final disposition are comprehensively reasoned by seven judges.

notes: Litigant-in-person appeal against strike-off; Twinsectra dishonesty test applied to practising certificate breaches.

enrichment.short_title: Yousef v Law Society: strike-off for dishonesty over practising certificate conditions
key_facts: Mrs Yousef worked for Malik & Malik without Office for the Supervision of Solicitors approval and without informing the firm of conditions on her practising certificate.
She had earlier been associated with a fraudulent solicitor and conditions were imposed following a prior tribunal decision.
She wrote to the Law Society claiming she had informed the firm, then admitted in a telephone call that she had not.
The tribunal found dishonesty under Twinsectra v Yardley and ordered strike-off.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by a litigant in person against a Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal decision striking her off the roll.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; strike-off upheld as necessary to protect the public and the profession; costs ordered not to be enforced without leave.
enrichment.ratio: Dishonesty in concealing practising certificate restrictions from an employer, established by the solicitor's own admissions, may warrant strike-off even where there was no client fund misappropriation and mitigation exists from past victimisation.
legal_issues: Whether dishonesty was properly found on the tribunal's facts
Appropriate sanction where breach related to practising conditions rather than client money
Application of the Twinsectra dishonesty test in professional discipline
Whether sympathy for personal and financial hardship should reduce the penalty
index_terms: Office for the Supervision of Solicitors

notes: Chesterton acquisition derivative claim appeal; Chadwick LJ refused CPR 19.9 permission after receivership.

enrichment.short_title: Jafari-Fini v Skillglass: refusal of derivative claim in Chesterton funding dispute
key_facts: Mr Jafari-Fini funded Phoenix Acquisitions' takeover of Chesterton International through a £12.85m Skillglass facility secured by debenture, guarantee and share charges.
Skillglass served default notices in October and December 2003; the validity of premature enforcement was disputed.
PAL could not repay the January 2004 tranche because Chesterton distributions under whitewash provisions were unavailable.
Chesterton entered administrative receivership in March 2005 before the derivative claim permission appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal of permission under CPR 19.9 to pursue derivative claims on behalf of PAL alongside personal claims.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; derivative claim refused but PAL may be added as defendant to be bound by preliminary issues in the personal action.
enrichment.ratio: Permission to bring a derivative claim should be refused where PAL had no realistic prospect of benefit from litigation because repayment depended on worthless Chesterton shares and the shareholder's personal action would determine the key issues.
legal_issues: Standing of a beneficial majority shareholder whose shares are registered in the alleged wrongdoer's name
Whether premature default notices amounted to repudiatory breach
Whether PAL could realistically have paid the January 2004 tranche absent alleged wrongdoing
Application of Barrett v Duckett principles under CPR 19.9
linked_authorities: Concord Trust v Law Debenture Corporation [2004] EWCA Civ 1001

notes: Dublin Convention transitional direct effect appeal; Article 11(5) one-month transfer rule held not individually enforceable.

enrichment.short_title: Omar v SSHD: Dublin Convention Article 11(5) in Regulation 343/2003 transitional period
key_facts: Mr Omar, a Somali national, claimed asylum in the UK on 9 June 2003 after entering Italy on 2 May 2003.
The UK requested Italy to take charge under the Dublin Convention; Italy accepted responsibility on 22 January 2004.
Removal directions were set for March 2004 more than one month after acceptance, allegedly breaching Article 11(5).
The asylum claim fell within the transitional period between the Regulation's entry into force and full application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from judicial review of certification as unfounded on third-country grounds and removal directions to Italy.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Article 29 of the Regulation gave direct effect only to Dublin criteria in Articles 4-8, not to Article 11(5) transfer timing mechanisms.
enrichment.ratio: During the Article 29 transitional period the Regulation directly applies only the Dublin Convention criteria for determining responsibility, not procedural mechanisms such as Article 11(5); even if breached, the remedy would be transfer to Italy not asylum determination in the UK.
legal_issues: Scope of direct effect of Regulation 343/2003 during the Article 29 transitional period
Distinction between Dublin Convention criteria and mechanisms
Whether breach of Article 11(5) shifts responsibility to the requesting Member State
Individual rights under inter-state asylum allocation conventions
linked_authorities: Zequiri v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2002] IMM AR 42

confidence.notes: Convention and Regulation analysis, Mitting J's reasoning and appellate conclusions are clearly articulated.

notes: Settlement boundary planning JR dismissed; inspector's rationalisation exception upheld under section 54A.

enrichment.short_title: Pembrokeshire v Welsh Assembly: challenge to outline dwelling outside settlement limit
key_facts: Pembrokeshire refused outline permission for a dwelling west of Green Grove, Princes Gate, because part of the site lay outside the settlement limit under Local Plan policy GEN03.
A planning inspector allowed the appeal, finding the proposal a reasonable rationalisation that would not materially harm countryside character.
The council challenged the inspector's departure from GEN03 under section 54A.
The Welsh Assembly defended the appeal decision as lawfully made.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of an inspector's decision allowing a planning appeal against refusal of outline permission.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the inspector lawfully identified a material consideration outweighing conflict with the development plan and was not irrational.
enrichment.ratio: A finding that development outside a settlement boundary would not materially encroach on countryside character and appearance is a material planning consideration capable of outweighing policy GEN03 under section 54A; weight is for the decision-maker unless perverse.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector had regard to the section 54A presumption in favour of the development plan
Whether absence of encroachment harm was a material consideration
Whether rationalisation of a tightly drawn settlement boundary could justify departure from GEN03
Wednesbury review of the inspector's balancing exercise
linked_authorities: City of Edinburgh Council v Secretary of State for Scotland [1997] 1 WLR 1447
Westminster City Council v Great Portland Estates plc [1985] 1 AC 661

confidence.notes: Inspector's reasoning, section 54A guidance and dismissal are clearly analysed though second refusal ground was not pursued.

notes: Family possession appeal; Jonathan Parker LJ refused Oxley v Hiscock point raised for first time on appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Kalidas v Kalidas: no permission to advance Oxley claim on family home appeal
key_facts: Bhik Kalidas, registered sole proprietor of 82 Hartford Road, sought possession against brothers Dilip and Satish who claimed equal one-third beneficial shares.
The property was bought in 1987 with family funds; Bhik redeemed the mortgage with a £70,000 loan in 1989 and was registered sole owner in 1991.
After their parents died in 1995 the brothers disputed occupation; the judge found no common intention of equal beneficial ownership.
On appeal the defendants sought to rely for the first time on Oxley v Hiscock for shares in the parents' interest only.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against a county court possession order dismissing a beneficial ownership counterclaim.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no real prospect of success on a new Oxley-based case not argued below and inconsistent with the judge's findings.
enrichment.ratio: A party cannot on appeal advance an entirely new constructive trust case under Oxley v Hiscock when the trial was fought on an express one-third common intention and the judge found no common intention of any beneficial interest for the defendants.
legal_issues: Whether Oxley v Hiscock could be raised for the first time on permission to appeal
Distinction between common intention as to occupation and as to beneficial ownership
Whether an alternative prayer for 'such shares as the court shall determine' permitted a new case
Prospects of retrial if permission were granted
linked_authorities: Lloyds Bank plc v Rosset [1991] 1 AC 107

confidence.notes: Judge's findings, new case on appeal reasoning and refusal are clearly explained.

notes: Supplementary judgment on Oakley design validity; ECJ reference and severability of Regulation 12.

enrichment.short_title: Oakley v Animal: registered design grace period and vires of 2001 Regulations
key_facts: Oakley applied to register a design after putting it into commercial use in the UK shortly before application.
Under the pre-harmonisation 1949 Act that use would invalidate registration; Regulation 12 of the 2001 Regulations preserved old law for existing registrations.
The Secretary of State was joined to appeal constitutional and EU law points on section 2(2) vires and transposition timing.
The judge referred to the ECJ whether Article 11.8 derogation could be exercised after the 28 October 2001 deadline.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Supplementary written reasons following a preliminary judgment on design validity and grace period law.
enrichment.outcome: If the ECJ rules the derogation could not be adopted after 28 October 2001, Regulation 12 would be ultra vires and severable, and Oakley's grace period would apply.
enrichment.ratio: Section 2(2) of the 1972 Act cannot authorise regulations achieving a result forbidden by Community law; if the ECJ holds the Article 11.8 derogation was time-barred, Regulation 12 is severable and the Directive's default grace period applies to affected registrations.
legal_issues: Vires of Regulation 12 under section 2(2) of the European Communities Act 1972
Whether Article 11.8 derogation had to be exercised by the Directive transposition deadline
Severability of Regulation 12 if partly invalid
Effect on Oakley's registered design if ECJ rules in its favour
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, Ex parte Salem [1999] 1 AC 450

confidence.notes: Supplementary reasons assume the main judgment; ECJ outcome remains unresolved at this stage.

notes: Cannabis factory custody time limit JR; Rose LJ upheld extension despite prosecution disclosure delays.

enrichment.short_title: Trinh v Southwark Crown Court: judicial review of custody time limit extension
key_facts: Mr Trinh and five co-accused were charged with conspiracy to produce cannabis following raids on suspected factories in June 2004.
Prosecution disclosure was late; surveillance videos served in September 2004 led to conflict of interest and new solicitors only weeks before trial.
HHJ McKinnon extended the custody time limit to 8 April 2005 for a trial fixed from 4 April.
The Crown conceded some dilatory conduct but contended good and sufficient cause existed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a Crown Court decision extending custody time limits under section 22(3) of the 1985 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the judge correctly applied the statutory test and was entitled to find good and sufficient cause despite prosecution delays.
enrichment.ratio: Due diligence under section 22(3) protects defendants from unjustified pre-trial detention rather than punishing administrative lapses; late video service does not necessarily prevent extension where causation of defence unreadiness is not established on the material before the court.
legal_issues: Correct test for extending custody time limits under section 22(3)
Whether prosecution dilatoriness precluded an extension
Causation between late video disclosure and change of solicitors
Procedural fairness and whether the judge should have heard evidence
linked_authorities: R v Crown Court at Manchester, ex parte McDonald [1999] 1 All ER 805

notes: Accountants' negligence appeal allowed on CPR 17.4; first-year delay allegations held same-fact amendments.

enrichment.short_title: Convergence v Vellacott: CPR 17.4 amendments for first-year accountancy negligence
key_facts: Convergence Group sued Chantrey Vellacott for unpaid fees; the accountants counterclaimed for negligence in a 1996-1999 group restructuring for the Marco Polo telecoms project.
The appellants sought to amend to plead negligence and delay in the first year from November 1996 to November 1997.
Master Price and Lloyd J held the amendments added a new time-barred claim not arising from substantially the same facts.
The pleaded case focused on defects from November 1997 onwards despite headings referring to services generally.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal of permission to re-amend a defence and counterclaim after expiry of limitation.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted and appeal allowed; proposed amendments met CPR 17.4(2) as a new claim arising from substantially the same facts of a single retainer and cumulative delay.
enrichment.ratio: Amendments alleging negligence during the first year of a continuous retainer for one restructuring project amount to a new claim under CPR 17.4 but arise from substantially the same facts as the pleaded cumulative delay case because they stem from the same retainer and already pleaded advice.
legal_issues: Whether first-year negligence amendments introduce a new claim under CPR 17.4
Construction of 'at all material times' and paragraphs 56-57 of the pleading
Whether new allegations arise from substantially the same facts as existing claims
Applicable permission test where part of the order is a second appeal
linked_authorities: Welsh Development Agency v Redpath Dorman Long Ltd [1994] 1 WLR 1409
Assicurazioni Generali SpA v Arab Insurance Group [2002] EWCA Civ 1642

notes: Kuwait Airways privilege appeal dismissed; fraud exception applies to litigation privilege after proven perjury.

enrichment.short_title: Kuwait Airways v Iraqi Airways: fraud exception to litigation privilege
key_facts: KAC sued IAC for wrongful interference with ten aircraft after the 1990 invasion of Kuwait; claims over the Mosul Four failed before Aikens J on causation.
David Steel J had already found in Perjury I that IAC used forgery and perjury to obtain state immunity and deceive the English courts.
In Perjury II KAC sought inspection of documents over which IAC claimed litigation privilege from earlier proceedings.
IAC argued the Cox and Railton fraud exception does not apply to litigation privilege once proceedings begin.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited appeal against an order requiring inspection of documents disclosed with a litigation privilege claim in ongoing proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the fraud exception applies to litigation privilege and inspection was properly ordered given established forgery and perjury.
enrichment.ratio: Communications brought into existence to further a criminal or fraudulent purpose, including perjury and conspiracy to deceive the court in litigation, are never protected by litigation privilege; the exception applies even after proceedings begin where fraud is established or strongly proved.
legal_issues: Whether the Cox and Railton fraud exception applies to litigation privilege
Standard of proof required before ordering inspection during ongoing litigation
Whether privilege survives where a prior judgment has found fraud on the court
Distinction between ordinary perjured denials and free-standing conspiracies to deceive
linked_authorities: R v Cox and Railton (1884) 14 QBD 153
R v Derby Magistrates' Court, ex parte B [1996] AC 487
Dubai Aluminium Co Ltd v Al Alawi [1999] 1 WLR 1964
